exercise.title: A whole key in one place
exercise.why: Every chord of a key has a shape inside any five frets of the neck, so you can change chord by changing shape and leave your hand where it is.

cells.text:
The three major chords of {{=key}} major meet in one area of the neck. {{chord:I}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}, here in the E shape. {{chord:IV}} is the 4th chord, built on {{4}}, in the A shape. {{chord:V}} is the 5th chord, built on {{5}}, in the C shape.
The necks below show the three in that order. Play each chord, and check that your hand stays over the same frets.
Practice until each change is a new shape and not a move along the neck.

Press a chord in the Chords row below to ring its notes in the position and hear it. These are the three minor chords of {{=key}} major, {{chord:ii}}, {{chord:iii}} and {{chord:vi}}, as three-note shapes on the G, B and high e strings in the same area.
Play each one straight after {{chord:I}}.
Practice until you can find all three without pressing the row.

Press Play below to start the metronome at {{=bpm}}, and strum the chord in the lit box, every one inside the same area of the neck.
If a chord sends your hand up the neck, stop and find its shape in the area before you go on.
{{?key}}In another key the area sits on other frets, and each chord keeps its shape inside it.
